sentences.text: The number was four thousand, nine hundred and eighty-three.
That is how many Greek men, in all of Constantinople, could be found who were fit to fight.
Add fewer than two thousand foreigners, Genoese, Venetians and others, and you get under seven thousand men for fourteen miles of walls.
Against them, about eighty thousand soldiers, plus a mass of irregulars.
The Venetian Barbaro wrote down a hundred and fifty thousand.
The Greeks, doing the arithmetic in their heads, said three or four hundred thousand.
Fear is a generous mathematician.
Help of a kind had arrived in late January.
A Genoese nobleman, Giovanni Giustiniani Longo, sailed in with about seven hundred armed men.
A professional soldier, a siege specialist.
The emperor put him in charge of the land walls.
One story says he was promised the island of Lemnos if the city held.
Whatever the terms, he took the worst job in the place: the Mesoteichion, the weak spot in the valley, which he held with something like two thousand men.
On the sixth of April, the bombardment began, and it went on, with a kind of ceaseless monotony, for more than six weeks.
The guns were clumsy.
They slid off their platforms in the April mud.
The big ones, Urban's included, could be fired just seven times a day.
But each of those seven shots did enormous damage.
Every night, the defenders came out and mended the wall with whatever they had: stones, timber, barrels, earth, hides.
Every morning, the guns knocked it down again.
A Venetian doctor named Nicolò Barbaro kept a diary of it all.
Then there was the harbor.
A great chain stretched across the mouth of the Golden Horn, held up on wooden floats, from a tower on the city side to one on the walls of Genoese Pera.
Ten ships guarded it.
As long as that chain held, the city's long sea walls along the harbor were safe, and the sultan's fleet was kept out.
On the twentieth of April, four ships, three Genoese and one loaded with grain for the emperor, came up from the south.
The Ottoman fleet went at them.

For hours it looked as though the four would be boarded and taken, with the sultan watching from the shore, shouting instructions about seamanship, a subject on which, we're told, he knew nothing at all.
Then the wind, which had died, came back.
The great sails filled, and the four ships crashed through the Turkish craft and into the harbor behind the chain.
Mehmed's admiral, Baltoghlu, was stripped of his rank and beaten with sticks.
The careful chronicler Critobulus counts a little over a hundred Turks dead that day, and twenty-two Christians.
The Archbishop of Mytilene, Leonard of Chios, says ten thousand Turks.
History is full of men whose arithmetic improves with distance.
That should have been the moment the siege turned.
It wasn't, because two days later Mehmed did something that isn't supposed to be possible.
He moved a navy over a hill.
At first light on Sunday, the twenty-second of April, the defenders looked across the harbor and saw ships.
Ottoman ships, inside the Golden Horn, behind the chain.

Somewhere between seventy and eighty light vessels had been hauled overland, up over the hill behind Galata, on wooden cradles and greased tracks, pulled by men and oxen and pulleys, in a single night.
All the while, the sultan's guns pounded the harbor so that the smoke and the noise would cover what was happening.
One account says the idea came from an Italian in his service.
Think about that for a moment.
The sultan's biggest gun, designed by a Hungarian or Wallachian.
His cleverest maneuver, perhaps suggested by an Italian.
Christendom, it turns out, was perfectly happy to sell the sultan its ideas, so long as the invoice cleared.
And now the defenders had to find more men for the harbor walls, from a pool of men that was already almost empty.
They tried to strike back.
On the twenty-eighth of April, a fire-raid on the Ottoman ships in the harbor went ahead, delayed at Genoese request, and by then the Turks were ready.
A boat was sunk, and some eighty or ninety men were lost.
Prisoners on both sides were executed in full view of the other.
Accusations flew, Venetians against Genoese, Genoese against Venetians, and Pears, writing in nineteen oh three, concluded that the Genoese were guilty of selfishness, but not of treason.
Then came the tunnels.
Ottoman miners dug under the walls at several points.
Inside the city, an engineer named John Grant dug counter-tunnels, met them underground, and wrecked them.
On the seventh of May, thirty thousand men attacked.
On the twelfth, fifty thousand.
Both were thrown back.
A great wooden tower the Turks rolled up on the eighteenth was burned by the defenders with gunpowder.
Each time, the city held.
Each time, it had fewer men to hold with.
Back on the third of May, a small ship had slipped out of the harbor to look for the Venetian relief fleet.
On the twenty-third, it came back.
It had found nothing.
The crew could have sailed for home.
They voted instead to return.
Whether the city be taken or not, one sailor said, whether it was to life or to death, their duty was to go back.
Hold on to that sentence.
A great deal of this story is about people who stayed.
And now, the city began to see signs.
During a procession, an icon of the Virgin slipped and fell.
A storm broke.
On the night of the full moon, the moon went dark for three hours.
Then a thick fog settled over Constantinople, and when it lifted, a strange light was seen shining on the dome of Hagia Sophia.
Some took it as the Holy Spirit leaving.
Some hoped it was the campfires of a Hungarian relief army.
Pears, writing about it in nineteen oh three, says it's hard to say which parts of the story are true and which are myth.
Some modern scholars suggest the red skies came from volcanic ash.
Whatever it was, the city read it as an answer.
Inside the walls, the quarrels never stopped.
Giustiniani had asked the grand duke, Loukas Notaras, for the cannon he controlled, to be moved to the Mesoteichion, where every gun was needed.
Notaras balked.
Leonard reports a bitter argument.
In the end, Giustiniani seems to have got his way.
But those were days, and the guns were precious, and the city had no days to spare.
Even on the eve of the final assault, the city could not stop being a city.
Barbaro describes Greek porters who were supposed to carry the wooden screens used to shield the defenders, and who stopped to demand their pay first.
You can read that as greed.
You can also read it as a population that had been promised things by its government for a very long time, and had stopped believing in them.
Both readings may be true.
Sieges are rarely noble in the details.

On Sunday, the twenty-seventh of May, the sultan rode through his whole army to announce that the great assault would come within two days, and, we're told, that his men would have three days of plunder.
The bombardment turned on the stockade across the Mesoteichion.
Three direct hits from the great cannon brought a section of it down.
Giustiniani was supervising the repairs when a splinter wounded him.
It was slight.
He had it dressed, and was back at his post before nightfall.
That was the Sunday.
On Monday, the twenty-eighth, the guns went quiet.
The Ottoman camp prepared.
The city prayed.
And a little after midnight, the drums began.
